stemMd: Why does a phospholipid bilayer form spontaneously when suitable phospholipids are dispersed in water?

options.label: A
options.textMd: The tails form peptide bonds with each other.

options.label: B
options.textMd: The heads are excluded from contact with water.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Water converts the fatty-acid chains into proteins.

options.label: D
options.textMd: The polar heads contact water while the nonpolar tails cluster away from it.

options.label: E
options.textMd: Every phospholipid becomes electrically neutral by losing phosphate.

explanationMd: Phospholipids are amphipathic: their heads are hydrophilic and their tails hydrophobic. A bilayer places the heads at the two aqueous surfaces and shields most tails inside. The arrangement is maintained mainly by noncovalent interactions rather than a new network of peptide bonds.

distractorRationale.a: Phospholipid assembly does not require peptide bond formation.
distractorRationale.e: The phosphate-containing heads remain part of the molecules.
distractorRationale.b: Polar heads interact favourably with water.
distractorRationale.c: No such chemical conversion explains bilayer assembly.
